messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Damian, a 32-year-old tutor, had been married for four years when the stalking began. It started subtly—a former student, a young man whose anger over a poor grade had been intense but seemed to blow over. Then came the late-night emails, the car idling outside their home, the figure he’d glimpse in his peripheral vision while walking to the grocery store. The worst moment was the night he found a note on his windshield, written in a jagged hand, telling him he would be sorry. Damian’s heart had seized; he’d felt watched, pinned, as if the world had shrunk to a single, threatening point. The police were called, a restraining order was filed, and the man eventually stopped. But for Damian, the world never quite expanded back to its normal size. Months later, the smallest things could pull him back into that night. Hearing a motorcycle revving on his street—the same sound that had preceded the idling car—would make his stomach clench, and he would immediately feel a familiar, creeping certainty that people are not what they seem, that anyone could be hiding a dangerous agenda. When a colleague expressed frustration about a scheduling conflict, even calmly, Damian’s mind would race: *He’s angry. He’s not what he seems. I can’t trust that I will do the right thing.* This self-doubt, this corrosive mistrust, had become a constant companion. He had come to believe that his own judgment was fundamentally broken—after all, he had once trusted that student. Because he was now certain that he couldn't trust his own judgment, almost anything could become a signal — a door that closed too loudly, a stranger who glanced his way a moment too long, a car that slowed even slightly near his home. Because he was certain he couldn’t trust his own perceptions, Damian began to avoid anything that felt like a test of his judgment. He stopped accepting new tutoring clients who lived in parts of town he didn’t know, reasoning that he simply could not assess the danger in unfamiliar places. He told his wife he was too tired for date nights, avoiding the emotional closeness that might force him to reveal how broken he felt. Even relaxing felt dangerous, a lapse in vigilance that could invite another threat. He had started telling himself, late at night when sleep wouldn’t come, that he deserved to suffer for having been so naive. He would lie awake, his ears straining for the sound of an engine, his body braced for a threat that wasn’t there. This constant hypervigilance took a toll. He often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong—a sudden knock at the door would send his heart racing, and he’d freeze, scanning the room for exits. His wife had started sleeping in the guest room because his constant tossing and his whispered alarms about noises she couldn’t hear left them both exhausted. The sleep problems became a cycle of their own: the more tired he was, the more his mind wandered back to the note on the windshield, and the more he felt that he was being followed—even when he was alone in his own living room. That feeling of being tracked would then spike his distrust again, confirming his belief that the world was full of hidden threats. Living in that constant state of felt threat, he found that ordinary things became triggers he couldn't ignore — a mailbox he'd left open, a neighbor's footsteps on the stairs, a shadow that passed across the window. But because he had never once stayed in a situation long enough to discover it was safe, his body had never learned that the danger was over — the threat remained as high and real as it had been the night he found the note. He had, on more than one occasion, cancelled a tutoring session last minute because he convinced himself he saw the former student’s car down the block, even though he knew, logically, the man was in another state. He had also stopped driving near the community college where it had all started. What finally brought Damian to seek help was a moment that frightened him more than the original stalking. Last week, he had snapped at a student who asked a simple question, his voice sharp and accusatory. The student, a kind young woman, had looked hurt and confused. Damian had seen his own fear in her eyes, and he had realized, with a sickening clarity, that the person he had become was someone he didn’t recognize. He is terrified that his marriage is fraying beyond repair, and that his career—the one thing he had always been good at—is now a source of daily dread. He is hoping, more than anything, to learn how to stop feeling like a target in a world that has, objectively, moved on.
